learningObjective: Reason about how a runtime handles dynamic (unknown-at-compile-time) shapes: symbolic dim tracking, allocator reservation, and specialization vs generalization trade-offs.

canonicalClaims.claim: Modern ML runtimes carry symbolic dim descriptors, declare supported shape ranges at build time, and use bucketing or optimization profiles to trade off build cost against runtime flexibility. Dynamic-shape kernels typically have some overhead compared to fully specialized ones.
conditions: The runtime supports declared shape ranges (min/opt/max or symbolic vars).
Deployment workload has some shape variability.
nonImplications: Does not imply the dynamic-static gap is always large.
Does not imply bucketing scales to arbitrary variability.

misconceptions.claim: Dynamic-shape kernels are exactly as fast as static-shape kernels.
misconceptions.whyWrong: Bounds checks, mask handling, and looser tile shapes can add overhead relative to fully specialized kernels.
Each bucket increases build cost; bucketing trades runtime flexibility for build cost.

misconceptions.claim: Inputs outside declared shape ranges are silently accepted.
misconceptions.whyWrong: Out-of-range shapes trigger fallback, recompilation, or error depending on the stack.

misconceptions.claim: Symbolic dims are just Python metadata with no compile-time effect.
misconceptions.whyWrong: Symbolic dims propagate through shape inference and constrain kernel selection and memory planning.
